title: Music and Emotion
objective: After this level you can explain why music can make us feel happy or sad.
summary: Music borrows the voice's code: sad is slow, soft and low. Culture tunes cues like major and minor. Sad songs please when safe, and a few people get little joy from music.

cards.headline: A piece with no words can still sound heartbroken.
cards.body: Nobody in a cello solo sings "I'm sad." There are no words at all. So how can a few notes sound like grief? Part of the answer is older than any song. It's in the way people talk.

cards.headline: Music speaks in the voice's code
cards.body: A 2003 review pooled 104 studies of emotional voices and 41 of music performance, and found the two use similar cues. Sadness comes out slow, soft and low, in speech and in music alike. Happiness comes out fast, loud and high. So when a cello sounds heartbroken, it's doing what a sad voice does. You already speak this language; music just sings it.

mascot.line: If you remember one thing: music borrows the voice's code. Slow, soft and low sounds sad.

cards.headline: Culture tunes some of the code
cards.body: Not every cue works that way. Remember Level 7: young children first judged happy and sad music by tempo alone, and only later by major and minor. And in Papua New Guinea, hearing major as happier was strongly tied to how much Western-style music people knew. Speed seems to speak early and widely; the mood of a minor key is partly learned.

cards.headline: Why a sad song can feel good
cards.body: Here's the puzzle: why would anyone choose to feel sad? A 2015 review found sadness from music is enjoyed when it feels non-threatening, when the music is beautiful, and when it helps, for example by easing a mood. The key is that in art, the real loss isn't there. A sad song lets you feel the storm from indoors.

cards.fact: Some people with normal hearing get little pleasure from music.
cards.context: A 2014 study described healthy people who heard music normally but got little pleasure from it, and their bodies showed no response to music others loved. Yet winning money pleased them just fine. Remember Level 91's musical chills? For them, music simply doesn't deliver that reward.

cards.headline: Music and emotion: felt
learned: Music borrows the voice's code: sad is slow, soft and low
Some cues, like major and minor, are partly learned
Sad music pleases when it's safe, beautiful and helpful
A few people get little pleasure from music at all

questions.prompt: According to the 2003 review of voice and music studies, how is sadness usually expressed in both?
questions.explanation: In voices and music alike, sadness tends to be slow, soft and low; happiness fast, loud and high.

questions.prompt: According to a 2015 review, why can listening to a sad song actually feel good?

options.label: Sad songs are secretly in major keys
options.rationale: Mode isn't the explanation the review gives.

options.label: Its sadness is safe and can ease a mood
Sad songs never cause real sadness
options.rationale: They do evoke sadness; it's just enjoyed.

options.label: Sad music always has a fast tempo
options.rationale: Sad music tends to be slow.

questions.explanation: Sadness from music is enjoyed when it is non-threatening, beautiful and helpful, as with easing a mood, because the real loss is absent.

questions.prompt: From Level 6: what do the Tsimane' and people with musical anhedonia both show?

options.label: Dissonant chords sound unpleasant to every listener alike
options.rationale: The Tsimane' liked dissonant chords as much as consonant ones.

options.label: Their hearing is damaged at high pitches
Hearing music and enjoying it are different things
Pleasure depends only on the notes being played
options.rationale: Both show the listener matters, not just the notes.

questions.explanation: The Tsimane' told consonant from dissonant chords yet liked both equally, and people with musical anhedonia hear music normally but get little pleasure from it.
